newsitem.title: UK: S&P affirms Munich Re, ups American Re ratings.
newsitem.headline: S&P affirms Munich Re, ups American Re ratings.

text.p: Standard & Poor's said on Tuesday it had affirmed the claims-paying ability ratings of Munich Reinsurance Company (Munich Re) and its Australian subsidiary Munich Reinsurance Co of Australia as AAA, and had removed both companies from Creditwatch negative, where they were placed on August 15, 1996.

At the same time S&P said it raised the claims-paying ability ratings of American Re-insurance Corporation (ARC) and its subsidiary American Alternative Insurance Corporation (AAIC) to AAA from AA and had removed ARC and AAIC from Creditwatch positive.

"ARC's subordinated debt rating and QUIPS (quarterly income preferred stock) rating are both raised to AA minus from A minus and BBB plus respectively," S&P said in a statement. "However, the outlook for the debt and preferred stock ratings is changed to negative from stable."
S&P said each of the above ratings was placed on Creditwatch in August 1996, when Munich Re announced its intention to buy ARC for approximately $3.3 billion.

"Following discussions with the management of both companies, and the completion of the purchase transaction, Standard & Poor's is satisfied that ARC and AAIC can immediately be considered strategically important to the Munich Re Group. Consequently the ratings of ARC and of AAIC now benefit from a degree of implied support from their new parent," S&P said.
The agency said Munich Re's existing U.S. subsidiary, which was expected to be merged into ARC, had hitherto been a middle-tier player in the important U.S. market.

"With its strong domestic market position, ARC furthers Munich Re's ambition to be a leading provider in every market in which it operates. The purchase also consolidates Munich Re's position as the leading global reinsurer, and provides Munich Re overnight with a significant business position and leading expertise in the growing field of financial reinsurance and alternative risk products," S&P said.

S&P said the affirmation of Munich Re's rating, and that of its Australian subsidiary, was based on a continuation of superior capitalisation, an improved business position and enhanced financial flexibility.

"The acquisition has weakened Munich Re's underlying capital strength, at least temporarily, as Standard & Poor's does not expect Munich Re to achieve an adequate payback on the substantial goodwill (approximately $2.44 billion) paid for ARC for some considerable time. Nevertheless, Standard & Poor's considers the capitalisation of the Munich Re Group to be as strong as it was prior to 1995."

S&P said Munich Re's superior business position had been further enhanced by the ARC purchase, but also by the exchange of holdings earlier this year with Allianz AG, which gave Munich Re 100 percent ownership of Deutsche Krankenversicherung, the leading German health insurer, in exchange for its partial holding in credit insurer Hermes Kreditversicherung.

"Financial flexibility, which was already very strong, has been further strengthened by the recent inclusion of Munich Re's shares in the German Dax index," S&P said. "However, Standard & Poor's considers that reported operating performance remains disappointing for a top-rated reinsurer; although Munich Re has reported record profits for 1995/6, it is not yet clear whether this is merely a cyclical improvement over what may be considered an unexceptional track record."

"This concern is the principal factor underlying the negative outlook for ARC's debt ratings, since the rating enhancement is dependent on the implied support of Munich Re and hence is linked to the parent's claims-paying ability rating," S&P said.
